title: E39 - AI vs Legacy SaaS in Legal: Min-Kyu Jung, CEO Ivo
author: Min-Kyu Jung

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Conditional optimism: User problems outrank AI branding
st.an: The source contains only closing remarks and promotional requests, with no substantive claims or evidence about user-led legal AI adoption, capability readiness, verification, market scenarios, or governance. Its position relative to the cluster therefore cannot be determined.

st.t: Contract intelligence: Business coordination exceeds document storage
st.an: Jung accepts the core proposition that contract technology should serve business-wide needs rather than function as a legal document repository. He materially develops it through an organisation-wide deployment model, company-specific context and playbooks, and an AI-led architecture that extracts intelligence without rigid metadata while potentially coexisting with incumbent CLM systems.
qs: Contracts are a business technology, not inherently a legal one.
So we're doing a contract intelligence rollout for Uber, and that's a rollout that we plan on doing across the entire organization.

st.t: Service model: AI challenges production more than lawyers
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s core view that AI is reorganising legal production rather than eliminating lawyers, and materially develops its buyer-side account. It explains why in-house contract AI should be designed around organisation-specific context and supplies a qualified customer example in which routine contract work shifted from outside counsel to AI, reducing external spend. Its evidence is mainly company-reported and anecdotal, consistent with the cluster’s caution about immature market-wide proof.
qs: And also, there's a much greater expectation of the depth of understanding you have about that organization versus a law firm.

But the ROI with Ivo in the case of that legal team is that a lot of that outside counsel spend is now evaporated, because why do you need to get a lawyer, a law firm, an extensive law firm to do like an NDA review when you can get Ivo to do it instead?

st.t: Vendor value: Concentration forecasts face diverse competition
st.an: The source adds Ivo as a concrete in-house legal-AI competitor and highlights the practical difficulty of shifting from legacy technology to an LLM-first product. This extends the cluster’s account of diverse competition, while offering no comparative performance or market-share evidence that would establish durable value capture or concentration.
qs: Ivo, as the founder will tell you, had to deal with a major transition between old legacy technology that they had built when they were just a four-person team and shifting over to an LLM AI first solution, which he describes as a challenge, even for a company that small but still doable.
But we are continuing to evaluate the key providers.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source accepts that AI value depends on selective, context-specific deployment rather than generic capability. It materially extends the cluster by showing how this applies to contract intelligence: products must encode an in-house organisation’s negotiating positions, risk tolerances and business relationships, preserve oversight for non-lawyer use, and be repeatedly redesigned as model capabilities change. Its efficiency and adoption claims are mainly company-supplied rather than independent evidence.
qs: They don't know what your preferred and alternative negotiating positions are, where the risk tolerances are, what deals are particularly important, and what supplier relationships are critical to the business.

And now, things have changed so, so much that's really leading to us having to reinvent multiple parts of our product over and over and over again, in a way that I don't think companies and normal size companies have had to do to the same degree.

st.t: Contract infrastructure: AI challenges siloed CLM systems
st.an: The source supports the synthesis by distinguishing enduring contract-management needs from legacy CLM products’ weaknesses. It argues that AI is pressuring CLM budgets and architecture while presenting fundamental rebuilding—not inevitable disappearance—as a plausible route to recovery; its product and adoption claims remain vendor-reported rather than comparative evidence.
qs: So CLM companies definitely solve very important problems.
And if that happens, I definitely wouldn't count out CLMs from making a big comeback.

st.t: In-house adoption: Stronger buyers may insource selectively
st.an: Jung directly supports the proposition that in-house AI can substitute for outside counsel in selected routine work and strengthen corporate legal departments as buyers. He also treats the effect as company-dependent rather than predicting universal outside-counsel decline, while advocating dedicated in-house products built around organisational context.
qs: So I think the first one is that part of the ROI that we're able to demonstrate to our clients is you're able to reduce outside council spend if you use Ivo.
It's very company, it's very dependent on the company.

st.t: Legal software: Workflow layers defend specialist value
st.an: Jung directly supports the cluster’s core claim that stronger LLMs made legal applications commercially viable while specialist value remains in product and workflow design rather than the foundation model alone. His dismissible-recommendation framing also aligns with a lawyer-controlled copilot, though the evidence is founder experience and early user feedback rather than comparative evaluation.
qs: It's not just a matter of you plug in the model and the product is great and the products are undifferentiated and the model is doing all of the work.
There's actually quite a lot of craftsmanship that goes into building these great products aside from the model itself.

kp.k: GPT-4 marked commercial viability for contract AI
kp.d: Jung argues that pre-LLM technology could not deliver Ivo's intended product and that its original offering lacked product-market fit. He identifies GPT-4 as the industry's commercial starting point, while crediting ChatGPT with making near-term feasibility apparent. His criticism of first-generation contract tools is qualified: they were not useful for his own legal work, though they may have helped with narrower tasks.
qs: So the original version of what we built was just pre-LLM and we didn't have a product market fit as a result.
But yeah, I would say GPT-4 then as I mentioned earlier, was probably the starting gun for the industry. That's when they really became commercially viable.
I'm sure they were probably useful across some narrow domain of tasks, but at least for the kind of work that I did, they weren't useful

kp.k: Application design differentiates products beyond underlying models
kp.d: Jung says a conversation with Nat Friedman about GitHub Copilot inspired his legal redlining prototype. He reports Friedman's account that coding autocomplete tolerated recommendations being wrong 70% of the time when suggestions arrived quickly and were easy to dismiss. This is a reported coding-product example, not a legal accuracy measurement or a recommendation to accept that error rate in legal work; Jung draws the broader lesson that application design matters independently of model capability.
qs: They were wrong like 70% of the time.
So what they discovered is people didn't mind if the recommendations were bad, as long as the recommendations came very quickly and you could dismiss the recommendations easily.
There's actually quite a lot of craftsmanship that goes into building these great products aside from the model itself.

kp.k: Customer payment triggered abandonment of legacy workflow software
kp.d: Jung recounts sharply divided lawyer reactions to an LLM-powered Word redlining prototype, with negative feedback dominant but five or six people asking to invest. A customer's willingness to pay before development in 2023 supplied the decisive signal to prioritize it over an existing revenue-generating contracting workflow product. He attributes the ability to pivot partly to a team of three or four people and frames the decision as overcoming sunk-cost attachment.
qs: And I had probably five or six different people just tell me after meeting with them, hey, can I be an investor in your company?
And that company became our first customer. And this was in 2023.
There was a contracting solution that, it wasn't a CLM, but it was sort of like a workflow contracting tool.
The smaller the team is, the easier it is to make those adjustments

kp.k: Rapid model progress requires repeated product reinvention
kp.d: Jung describes new models or techniques emerging every three or six months and changing feasible product experiences. Early GPT-4's 8,000-token context window and difficulty with nested contractual logic constrained Ivo's design, especially exclusions and limitations of liability. He says subsequent improvements have required repeated redesign rather than a one-time transition to AI.
qs: every three or six months, some new model emerges or some new, I don't know, RLHF technique emerges or whatever it is.
we were really constrained by what was possible with GPT-4 and the fact that you had a context window of 8,000 tokens.
You couldn't do any multiple nested layers of logic, like exclusions and limitations of liability were almost impossible to figure out.
that's really leading to us having to reinvent multiple parts of our product over and over and over again

kp.k: Model progress may delay buyers' adoption decisions
kp.d: Abramowitz argues that uncertainty about capabilities six months ahead can discourage both buying and building, creating analysis paralysis. He speculates that a transformer-model plateau could increase adoption. Jung agrees that rapidly shifting vendor categories and unclear product boundaries make purchasing decisions harder; neither speaker supplies systematic adoption evidence.
qs: I have argued recently that AI model progress actually hinders AI adoption.
And that question mark can often lead to analysis paralysis, just dragging your heels and doing nothing.
at some point, these models, at least the transformer model, may plateau. And I think in those instances, we may actually see more adoption at that point than less.
the category seems to be shifting so fast. It does make decisions like that more challenging.

kp.k: In-house specialization reflects distinct products and commercial incentives
kp.d: Jung says Ivo exclusively serves in-house teams, with revenue weighted toward large enterprises and Fortune 500 companies, naming IBM, Uber and Shopify. He argues that law firms and legal departments require fundamentally different best-in-class products. He also identifies a strategic conflict between helping law firms earn more and helping corporate buyers reduce outside counsel spending, choosing the latter.
qs: we exclusively work with in-house legal teams
companies like IBM or Uber or Shopify, and Fortune 500 is where our sweet spot tends to be.
we really believe that those are two very fundamentally different markets and the best in class product looks different for both.

if you serve the law firms, the argument is we can help you make more money. And if you serve in-house legal teams, the argument is we can help you save money by not having to spend it on our law firms.

kp.k: Contract AI can substitute for routine outside counsel work
kp.d: Jung says outside counsel remain involved in commercial contracting, with substantial variation across companies. He recounts a conversation the previous day with a lawyer at an unnamed Canadian company whose small internal team relies on law firms during busy periods to avoid layoffs in downturns. He reports reduced outside counsel spending through Ivo and carries the customer's opinion that Ivo performed better on average than her law firms. This is a vendor-reported customer anecdote, not an independently measured quality comparison or quantified spending study.
qs: a pretty significant volume of their routine contract work is actually handled by outside law firms.
they want to keep their team pretty small. So in downtimes, they don't have to lay anyone off, and in uptimes, they rely on outside counsel to make up the balance.
a lot of that outside counsel spend is now evaporated
her opinion was that Ivo was better on average than the law firms that she's been working with.

kp.k: Institutional context is central to enterprise legal AI
kp.d: Jung characterizes generic AI tools as capable junior lawyers lacking organizational onboarding. In-house lawyers' single-client focus and repetitive agreements make business priorities, risk tolerances, negotiation positions and supplier relationships important inputs. He presents granular playbooks and customization as differentiators, particularly where hundreds of lawyers need consistency. He claims approximately an 85% head-to-head trial win rate in competitive selections involving 5, 10 or sometimes 20 vendors, without giving a sample size, period or evaluation methodology.
qs: we have something like an 85% head-to-head trial win rate.
Every single deal we go into is a competitive process where 5, 10, sometimes 20 vendors are being evaluated before we end up being selected.
they're like a smart junior lawyer who joined your company five minutes ago and have no context whatsoever about what your company does.

They don't know what your preferred and alternative negotiating positions are, where the risk tolerances are, what deals are particularly important, and what supplier relationships are critical to the business.
we went really deep into building out functionality that allows quite granular customization down to the detail of, do you like to use Oxford commas or not?

kp.k: Contract intelligence extends beyond the legal department
kp.d: Jung distinguishes a contracting company from a legal company, identifying procurement and sales as adjacent users; Abramowitz adds finance and accounting. Jung reports an Uber contract-intelligence rollout planned across the entire organization. He argues that serving non-lawyers requires different product design to balance reduced legal-team workload against lawyers' concerns about unsupervised contract activity, and that law-firm customer demands can divert development away from these uses.
qs: Contracts are a business technology, not inherently a legal one.
we're doing a contract intelligence rollout for Uber, and that's a rollout that we plan on doing across the entire organization.

They love it because it means they don't have to spend all of their time doing it. But they hate it because they're scared of the idea of a salesperson going crazy with a contract that they have no oversight for.

kp.k: AI competes with CLM for budgets and implementation capacity
kp.d: Jung agrees that CLM-led purchasing is happening less, explaining that even products without directly overlapping functions compete for legal operations budgets and teams' capacity to evaluate and onboard systems. Abramowitz takes a stronger position, saying he would not recommend buying a CLM today and asserting that AI alternatives offer lower prices, easier implementation and greater ROI. The host discloses an Agiloft shareholding arising from the Term Scout transaction; these remain speaker assessments rather than comparative cost evidence.
qs: even if CLMs are not a direct competitor to a lot of the legal AI tools, they are competing often for the same dollars in the budget
often competing for just the capacity a team has to evaluate a lot of different solutions and on-board different solutions at the same time.
I'm by virtue of the Term Scout Agilof deal, I'm a holder in Agilof stock.
I wouldn't recommend to any legal department today to buy a CLM.

kp.k: Rigid metadata limits traditional contract repositories
kp.d: Jung argues that CLMs borrowed CRM-style structures ill-suited to contracts because future information needs cannot be fully anticipated through predefined metadata. He cites unexpected pandemic-related questions and tariff pass-through questions as examples. He claims Ivo can analyze millions of agreements without metadata tagging, account for relationships between agreements, and gain adoption within companies already using sophisticated CLMs. These are product capability and uptake claims, not independently demonstrated findings.
qs: I think I had the feeling that the CLM products are built using CRM systems as an analogy.
It's often not obvious until retrospect what information you want.
Now, we have to worry about, can we pass on the cost of tariffs to our customers?
We can extract intelligence at scale across millions of agreements. We can do it without any metadata tagging.
We understand relationships between different agreements as well, and we use that information to help inform the analysis we give.

kp.k: Legacy CLM recovery requires fundamental AI-oriented redesign
kp.d: Jung does not write off CLM incumbents: he argues that they address important problems but face an innovator's dilemma because existing products are poorly suited to AI. His recommendation is to rethink products from the ground up rather than preserve existing designs. He presents a comeback as conditional on leaders overcoming the inertia associated with established revenue and products.
qs: CLM companies definitely solve very important problems.
I think they're in an innovator's dilemma scenario where the tools that they've built are just not well suited for the world of AI.
the leaders there need to have the courage to kind of rip out what they're doing at the moment already and kind of rethink from the ground up
if that happens, I definitely wouldn't count out CLMs from making a big comeback.

kp.k: ROI extends from lawyer time to business speed
kp.d: Jung says efficiency remains the dominant ROI consideration, separating lawyer-hours saved from organization-wide gains through faster contracting. He reports that one unnamed customer reduced average NDA turnaround from approximately four days to one day, tracked through its CLM as a business KPI. He argues that this can accelerate projects and sales, while acknowledging that the monetary value of broader business acceleration is harder to quantify.
qs: The main one, by far, the dominant consideration is efficiency.
we have a customer who told us they've gone from, I think, something like four days on average to turn around an NDA down to one day.
they use CLM to track turnaround times.

that is slightly harder to quantify that value, but that is where I think a lot of the value comes from, which is we can make your legal team so much more efficient and that makes your business a lot faster.

kp.k: Contract intelligence enables previously uneconomic organizational knowledge
kp.d: Jung argues that contract intelligence creates value beyond automating existing research because manual extraction is often too costly to undertake at all. Proposed benefits include identifying risk and departures from standard terms, informing renegotiation at renewal, and giving new lawyers context about longstanding supplier relationships and customary concessions. He explicitly describes this value category as emerging and harder to translate into dollar terms.
qs: This is much fuzzier, but with the Contract Intelligence Tool, we can extract all kinds of really interesting insights from your database.
what's more common is that it's so cost prohibitive to get this information manually that it just doesn't happen.
it helps you understand risk across your agreements
there is a real value in just having a better sense of understanding what's actually in your contracts.
part of the work we're doing now is to help our clients understand what that value looks like on dollar terms

kp.k: Lawyer demand includes reassurance, not just task execution
kp.d: Reflecting on first-generation consumer contract review, Abramowitz argues that automating what lawyers do does not necessarily replace why clients hire them: reassurance from an attentive professional with demanding standards. Separately, he speculates that strong reactions to AI can reflect challenges to core beliefs about human distinctiveness, not only employment insecurity. These are the host's interpretations, not measured client or lawyer attitudes.
qs: there is a difference very often between what a lawyer does and why you hire a lawyer
You hire a lawyer because you want to be able to sleep at night.
Someone with like very serious professional standards
it actually challenges some of like their core beliefs about the world

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Jung identifies GPT-4 as the commercial viability threshold for legal AI and argues that subsequent model improvements repeatedly change what legal products can do.
pts.d: Min-Kyu Jung contrasts earlier tools, which he found unhelpful for his own legal work, with LLM-based products. He says improved models have required Ivo to reinvent product components previously designed around GPT-4's limited context window and difficulties with nested contractual logic. He also argues that application design, rather than the underlying model alone, differentiates products.

pts.k: Jung claims that in-house contract AI can reduce outside-counsel expenditure and make law firms less central to routine contracting.
pts.d: He presents reduced external legal spending as part of Ivo's ROI and strategic reason for serving in-house departments exclusively. His example concerns a Canadian company using outside counsel to accommodate fluctuating workloads without increasing permanent headcount. He reports that Ivo displaced substantial spending and that the company's lawyer considered it better on average than its external firms. That quality comparison is a customer opinion relayed by Jung, not a measured comparison.

pts.k: Jung argues that effective in-house AI requires organisation-specific knowledge and a different product from law-firm AI.
pts.d: He describes an 'onboarding problem': a generally capable AI lacks the company's negotiating preferences, risk tolerances, priorities and relationships. He says Ivo addresses this through granular playbook-based redlining and customisation, particularly for large departments needing consistency. He treats the distinction between law-firm and in-house markets as foundational to product strategy, rather than assuming redlining requirements are interchangeable.

pts.k: Jung claims AI contract intelligence overcomes rigid metadata limitations and extends contract use beyond legal departments.
pts.d: He argues that conventional repositories cannot anticipate every future question about contracts, whereas Ivo can analyse agreements at scale without advance metadata tagging and take relationships between agreements into account. He describes adoption alongside existing CLM systems and an opportunity to serve procurement and sales teams, subject to product controls addressing lawyers' concerns about nonlawyer use.

pts.k: Jung says AI competes with CLM for organisational resources, while incumbent vendors may recover by rebuilding around AI.
pts.d: He agrees that CLM implementation demand is occurring less frequently and explains that AI and CLM compete for budgets and teams' evaluation and onboarding capacity, even when not direct substitutes. He characterises incumbent CLM vendors as facing an innovator's dilemma: their existing products are poorly suited to AI, but their revenue and organisational commitments make radical redesign difficult. He does not predict their inevitable disappearance.

pts.k: Jung describes AI's value as lawyer efficiency, faster business processes and access to contract insights previously too costly to obtain.
pts.d: He distinguishes individual time savings from organisation-level benefits, such as shorter NDA turnaround times enabling projects to begin sooner. He also claims contract intelligence can reveal risks, deviations from standard terms and relationship history that would otherwise remain unexamined. He explicitly acknowledges that assigning dollar values to these broader benefits is harder than calculating labour-time savings.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: Commercial traction and product-development claims rest principally on Jung's experience and company-reported indicators.
pts.d: Jung cites an early customer paying for the proposed LLM product in 2023, contrasting this with the difficulty of selling the preceding workflow product. He reports approximately an 85% head-to-head trial win rate in competitive procurement processes. The transcript supplies no sample size, trial protocol, time period or independently verified results; the win rate is a commercial selection metric, not a benchmark of legal accuracy. His observations about model limitations and repeated redesign come from building Ivo.

pts.k: ROI evidence consists of customer anecdotes, including a reported CLM-tracked reduction in NDA turnaround time.
pts.d: Jung reports one customer's approximate reduction from four days to one day and says its CLM records turnaround as a KPI. He offers a separate Canadian-company anecdote for outside-counsel substitution. No underlying records, spend amounts, comparison groups or generalisable productivity study are presented. Broader benefits from faster sales, improved risk visibility and relationship knowledge are proposed value mechanisms whose monetary measurement remains under development.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The account traces a late-2022 prototype and 2023 commercial pivot to ongoing, rapid product change at the time of the 2026 interview.
pts.d: Jung tentatively dates a prototype demonstration to December 2022 and identifies the first paying customer for the new product in 2023. He describes meaningful model or technique changes every three or six months. His claimed priority for AI redlining and playbook redlining is qualified by his knowledge, rather than asserted as independently established. He says a three- or four-person team made the initial pivot easier; continued willingness to pivot remains important as the company grows.

pts.k: Outside-counsel substitution varies by company; broader enterprise deployment and incumbent recovery remain conditional or prospective.
pts.d: Jung qualifies the extent of existing outsourcing as company-dependent, so the spending-reduction opportunity is not presented as uniform. Uber's organisation-wide rollout is described as planned, not completed. A CLM comeback depends on leaders rethinking and rebuilding products around AI; he gives no fixed deadline. Contract-intelligence value depends on extracting useful organisational context, with dollar-based ROI quantification still being developed.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The principal beneficiaries described are corporate legal departments, particularly large enterprises; external firms face reduced routine-work demand.
pts.d: Ivo is a software vendor serving the buyer side, not an ALSP delivering legal work. Jung says it serves in-house teams of all sizes, with revenue weighted toward large enterprises and a Fortune 500 sweet spot, naming IBM, Uber and Shopify. In-house lawyers gain capacity and contextual consistency; companies may spend less on outside counsel. The claims concern enterprise contracting rather than unmet public legal need or access to justice.

pts.k: AI also affects business teams, legal operations buyers and incumbent contracting-software providers.
pts.d: Procurement and sales teams are prospective users of contract intelligence beyond legal, while lawyers require oversight of nonlawyer interactions with agreements. Legal operations departments face competing demands on budgets and implementation capacity. Legacy CLM vendors face pressure to redesign products despite established revenue and organisational inertia; smaller vendors may be more agile.
